metadata.title: The Sentinel - Volume Thesis

sections.text: Three results from distributed computing theory set the floor for everything in this volume. If you remember nothing else, remember these:

metadata.concepts: [distributed systems, security engineering, cloud architecture, consensus, zero trust]
metadata.title: The Sentinel - Volume Thesis

sections.text: ### 1. FLP Impossibility (Fischer, Lynch, Paterson, 1985)

metadata.concepts: [distributed systems, security engineering, cloud architecture, consensus, zero trust]
metadata.title: The Sentinel - Volume Thesis

sections.text: No deterministic protocol can guarantee consensus in a fully asynchronous system if even one process can crash.

metadata.concepts: [distributed systems, security engineering, cloud architecture, consensus, zero trust]
metadata.title: The Sentinel - Volume Thesis

sections.text: This is not a practical limitation. It is a **proven impossibility** --- the same category as the halting problem. Every consensus protocol you encounter (Paxos, Raft, PBFT, Tendermint) works around FLP by weakening one of its assumptions: partial synchrony, failure detectors, randomization, or leader oracles.

metadata.concepts: [distributed systems, security engineering, cloud architecture, consensus, zero trust]
metadata.title: The Sentinel - Volume Thesis

sections.text:
```
FLP ASSUMPTION SET                      ESCAPE ROUTES
┌────────────────────────────────┐      ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. Fully asynchronous          │  ──► │ Partial synchrony (Paxos, Raft) │
│ 2. Deterministic protocol      │  ──► │ Randomization (Ben-Or)          │
│ 3. Even one crash failure      │  ──► │ Failure detectors (Chandra-T.)  │
│ 4. Agreement + validity +      │      │ Timeouts + leader election      │
│    termination all required    │      │   (practical systems)           │
└────────────────────────────────┘      └─────────────────────────────────┘
```

sections.text: ### 2. CAP Theorem (Brewer, 2000; Gilbert-Lynch proof, 2002)

metadata.concepts: [distributed systems, security engineering, cloud architecture, consensus, zero trust]
metadata.title: The Sentinel - Volume Thesis

sections.text: A distributed data store cannot simultaneously provide Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance. Since partitions are not optional in real networks, the actual choice is:

metadata.concepts: [distributed systems, security engineering, cloud architecture, consensus, zero trust]
metadata.title: The Sentinel - Volume Thesis

sections.text:
- **CP**: Reject requests during partition (preserve consistency). ZooKeeper, etcd, Spanner.
- **AP**: Serve possibly-stale data during partition (preserve availability). DynamoDB, Cassandra.

metadata.concepts: [distributed systems, security engineering, cloud architecture, consensus, zero trust]
metadata.title: The Sentinel - Volume Thesis

sections.text: CAP is a **theorem about network partitions**, not a general design philosophy. When no partition exists, you can have both C and A. The engineering question is: *what happens when the network breaks?*

metadata.concepts: [distributed systems, security engineering, cloud architecture, consensus, zero trust]
metadata.title: The Sentinel - Volume Thesis

sections.text: ### 3. Byzantine Fault Tolerance (Lamport, Shostak, Pease, 1982)

metadata.concepts: [distributed systems, security engineering, cloud architecture, consensus, zero trust]
metadata.title: The Sentinel - Volume Thesis

sections.text: A system of *n* nodes can tolerate *f* Byzantine (arbitrary/malicious) failures if and only if **n >= 3f + 1**. Byzantine faults are the worst case: a node can lie, send conflicting messages, collude, or stay silent.

metadata.concepts: [distributed systems, security engineering, cloud architecture, consensus, zero trust]
metadata.title: The Sentinel - Volume Thesis

metadata.concepts: [distributed systems, security engineering, cloud architecture, consensus, zero trust]
metadata.title: The Sentinel - Volume Thesis

sections.text:
Why 3f + 1?
  f nodes can lie.
  f nodes can be silent (crashed).
  You still need f + 1 honest, responsive nodes to form a majority.
  f + f + (f + 1) = 3f + 1.
```

metadata.concepts: [distributed systems, security engineering, cloud architecture, consensus, zero trust]
metadata.title: The Sentinel - Volume Thesis

sections.text: The security connection is direct: zero-trust architecture is the design posture that assumes *every component might be Byzantine*. Not because your own services are malicious, but because a compromised host, a stolen credential, or a MITM attacker produces the same observable behavior as a Byzantine node.

sections.text: ### The Mapping

metadata.concepts: [distributed systems, security engineering, cloud architecture, consensus, zero trust]
metadata.title: The Sentinel - Volume Thesis

sections.text:
| Concept | Distributed Systems | Security Engineering | Cloud Architecture |
|---------|--------------------|--------------------|-------------------|
| **Core problem** | Agreement without central authority | Trust without perimeter | Reliability without permanence |
| **Theoretical bound** | FLP impossibility | Rice's theorem (undecidable properties of programs) | CAP trade-offs on every design choice |
| **Protocol class** | Paxos, Raft, PBFT | TLS, OAuth 2.0, OIDC, mTLS | Load balancers, health checks, circuit breakers |
| **Failure assumption** | Nodes crash or go Byzantine | Adversaries are active | Infrastructure is ephemeral |
| **Redundancy model** | Replicas (leader + followers) | Defense in depth (layered controls) | AZs, regions, multi-cloud |
| **Quorum concept** | Majority of replicas agree | Multi-factor authentication, multi-party approval | Writes ack'd by majority of replicas |
| **Consistency model** | Linearizable, causal, eventual | Least privilege (no implicit access) | Strong consistency costs latency |
| **Partition response** | CP: reject / AP: serve stale | Network segmentation, microsegmentation | Failover to healthy region |
| **Verification** | Cryptographic signatures on votes | Zero-trust: verify every call | Health probes, readiness checks |
| **Rollback** | Log-based recovery, WAL | Incident response, forensic timeline | Blue/green deploy, rollback to last-known-good |

sections.text: For someone with MIT TCS background: Git's merge operation is a form of **operational transformation** on a CRDT (specifically, a Merkle DAG of immutable content-addressed objects). The "consensus" happens at `git push` time --- the remote acts as a linearization point. Git is eventually consistent by default, strongly consistent by convention (the blessed remote).
